doc_name: Palace of Justice of the Argentine Nation
text: The Palace of Justice of the Argentine Nation (Spanish: Palacio de Justicia de la Nación Argentina, commonly known locally as Palacio de Justicia or Palacio de Tribunales) is a large building complex located in Buenos Aires, Argentina, serving as the seat of the Supreme Court and other lower courts. Designed in a monumental Eclectic neoclassical style and constructed between 1905 and 1910, the building is a National Historic Landmark with a total floor area of 60,100 m² (647,000 sq ft). The original design was created by French architect Norbert Maillart in 1889 during the presidency of Miguel Juárez Celman, but construction was halted by the Baring crisis of 1890, delaying work for nearly 20 years. Construction resumed during the second presidency of Julio A. Roca, with approval for works granted in 1904 and construction beginning in 1905. A portion of the palace was inaugurated in 1910 by President José Figueroa Alcorta during the Centennial of the May Revolution, though the Supreme Court did not move into the building until 1912, when Maillart left both the project and Argentina. In 1914, due to the onset of World War I and administrative and budgetary issues, construction was suspended and later resumed in the 1920s. Around 1925, the original plan was modified to accommodate the growing Judicial Branch, resulting in the addition of an extra floor instead of the original mansard roof, and the inclusion of two statues crowning the façade that hold the tables of the law. Despite these changes, many interior details remained incomplete. The palace was not fully completed until 1942 and was declared a National Historic Monument of Argentina in 1999 via decree 349. Its facades are clad in imitation Paris stone, and it features interior sculptures such as Justice by Rogelio Yrurtia, a bust of José de San Martín by Luis Perlotti, and a replica of the flag of the Andes, designed by San Martín during the independence battles. The palace includes rooms such as the "Patio of Honor," where concerts were held, and the Audience Room of the Supreme Court of Justice. To design the façade ornaments, architect Virginio Colombo arrived from Milan and eventually settled in Buenos Aires, becoming a prominent figure in the local art nouveau movement.
